title: Monolith vs microservices vs modular monolith
scopeHtml: Scope: architecture styles, service mesh, API composition, migration.

notes.title: Monolith
notes.html:
A monolith is one deployable unit containing all features, usually with one database. Calls between modules are plain function calls.

Strengths: simple to build, test and debug (one stack trace); transactions across features are free (one DB transaction); fast calls (nanoseconds, not network milliseconds); one deploy pipeline; cheap to operate. Weaknesses: scaling is all-or-nothing, a bug or memory leak in one area can take down everything, large teams step on each other (merge conflicts, slow builds), tech stack is shared, deploys get risky as the codebase grows.

Worked example. A monolith on 4 identical 8-core instances behind a load balancer handles 6k requests/s. Cost: 4 instances. Splitting image-resizing out matters only if it eats CPU; otherwise you just scale the whole monolith horizontally (stateless, shared DB).

Industry examples. Stack Overflow served hundreds of millions of page views a month from a handful of web servers; Shopify runs one of the largest Ruby on Rails monoliths (a "modular monolith"); Basecamp and GitHub (largely Rails for years) show monoliths scale far; Instagram started as a Django monolith.

Decision gravity. Starting with a monolith is reversible and the cheapest path; premature microservices is the expensive one-way door. Breaks when: team size exceeds roughly 30 to 50 engineers in one codebase, deploys block each other, or one part needs a different scaling shape.

Everyday analogy. A single food truck where one person cooks, serves and cleans: efficient and easy at small scale.

Common interview traps.

  • Calling a monolith "legacy" or "bad". It is a valid, often optimal choice.
  • Forgetting a monolith can still scale horizontally behind a load balancer.

notes.title: Microservices
notes.html:
Microservices split the system into many small services, each owning its data, deployed and scaled independently, talking over the network. The aim is organisational independence: a team owns a service end to end.

Mechanism: services expose APIs (REST/gRPC) or events (Kafka); each owns its database (no shared tables); you need service discovery, API gateway, centralised logging, distributed tracing, CI/CD per service, and resilience patterns (timeouts, retries with backoff, circuit breakers, bulkheads).

Worked example (the latency tax). A request touching 6 services in a chain, each p99 = 50 ms, has a combined p99 well above 50 ms; if each service has 99.9% availability, the chain is 0.999^6 = 99.4% (about 52 hours of downtime/year vs 8.8 hours for one). Add retries carelessly and a slow dependency causes a retry storm.

Industry examples. Amazon ("two-pizza teams", thousands of services), Netflix (about 1,000 microservices, Hystrix/Resilience4j, Eureka, Zuul), Uber (about 2,000+ services, later "domain-oriented microservices" to tame sprawl), Spotify squads. Segment and Istio moved some services back to monoliths (a well-known "back to monolith" story is Amazon Prime Video's video monitoring tool, 2023, which cut cost by ~90% by merging components; confirm details).

Decision gravity. A one-way door: splitting data across services is easy; merging it back is painful. It also needs platform investment (observability, deployment, on-call). Choose it for team scaling and independent scaling, not for "modernity".

Everyday analogy. A food court: each stall owns its kitchen and menu; you can add stalls without closing others, but you need signs, a cashier system and cleaners shared across all.

Common interview traps.

  • Splitting by technical layer (UI service, DB service) instead of business capability.
  • Shared database across services (a distributed monolith).
  • Forgetting the operational costs: tracing, versioning, contract tests, on-call.
  • Synchronous call chains causing cascading failures.

notes.title: Modular monolith
notes.html:
A modular monolith is one deployable with strict internal module boundaries; each module owns its code and its tables, and talks to others through a public interface. It captures most benefits of microservices without the network.

Mechanism: package per business domain (orders, billing, catalog); only an api package is public; dependencies enforced by tools (ArchUnit in Java, Gradle/Maven modules, Kotlin internal, Nx boundaries). Separate schemas or table prefixes per module and no cross-module joins or foreign keys; cross-module communication through interfaces or in-process events. Later, any module with a hard boundary can be extracted into a service.

// orders/api/OrderApi.kt  (public)
interface OrderApi { fun place(cmd: PlaceOrder): OrderId }
// billing depends only on orders.api, never on orders.internal
class BillingListener(private val orders: OrderApi) { /* ... */ }
// ArchUnit rule: modules may only use each other's api package
noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..billing..")
  .should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAPackage("..orders.internal..").check(classes);

Worked example. 40 engineers, 6 modules, 1 deploy a day. Local calls cost nothing, one DB transaction keeps orders and billing consistent. When search needs independent scaling, extract it behind its existing interface in a week, not months.

Industry examples. Shopify (components with enforced boundaries, "Packwerk"), Google's monorepo with strict visibility rules, Spring Modulith, Basecamp. Many "microservices regrets" end here.

Decision gravity. Cheap and reversible; the best default for teams of 10 to 100. Boundaries drawn wrong are cheap to redraw inside a monolith and very expensive across services.

Everyday analogy. An apartment building: separate flats with locked doors and a shared lobby, one roof and one boiler.

Common interview traps.

  • Boundaries only on paper; without enforcement, modules turn into a big ball of mud.
  • Sharing tables between modules.

notes.title: How to choose
notes.html:
Choose by team size, independent scaling needs, and operational maturity.

Monolith Modular monolith Microservices
Team size 1 to 15 10 to 100 50+ with platform team
Deploy One One Many, independent
Transactions Local ACID Local ACID Sagas, eventual
Latency Lowest Lowest Network hops
Ops cost Lowest Low High
Fault isolation Poor Poor Good
Scale granularity Whole app Whole app Per service

Triggers to extract a service: a different scaling profile (CPU-heavy video encoding), different availability needs (payments), different tech (ML in Python), different release cadence, a team boundary, regulatory isolation (PCI scope).

Worked example. Photo-sharing app: the monolith handles feeds fine, but image processing needs GPUs and spikes 10x. Extract only media-processing as a worker service fed by a queue; everything else stays in the monolith.

Industry examples. Etsy, Shopify and Airbnb all evolved: monolith, then selective services. Segment's "goodbye microservices" post and Amazon Prime Video's consolidation show overshooting.

Decision gravity. Start modular; extract on evidence. Splitting is one-way, merging is expensive, so each extraction needs a business reason and an owner.

Everyday analogy. Start with one shop; open a separate warehouse only when the shop can no longer store and ship at once.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "microservices" without stating team size, scale numbers or trade-offs.
  • Ignoring that a distributed monolith (services that deploy together) has the costs of both.

notes.title: Decomposition and migration (strangler fig)
notes.html:
Migrate gradually: route traffic through a facade and replace one slice at a time, never a big-bang rewrite. The strangler fig pattern wraps the old system while new services grow around it.

Mechanism: put a proxy/gateway in front; for each capability, build the new service, route a small percentage of traffic (1%, 10%, 100%) to it, compare results (shadow traffic, dark launches), then delete the old code. Data migration: first read-through, then dual-write with reconciliation or CDC, then flip ownership. Use anti-corruption layers so the new model is not polluted by the old schema. Pick seams by bounded contexts (Domain-Driven Design): high cohesion inside, loose coupling outside.

location /billing/ { proxy_pass http://new-billing; }   # migrated
location / { proxy_pass http://legacy; }                # everything else

Worked example. Migrate billing: week 1 build service and replicate data with Debezium; week 3 shadow-read 100% and diff (0.02% mismatches fixed); week 5 route 5% writes; week 7 100%; week 9 delete monolith code. Rollback at any point is a routing change.

Industry examples. Martin Fowler named the pattern; Amazon retired its monolith (Obidos) gradually; Netflix migrated from a datacenter monolith to AWS microservices over about 7 years after a 2008 database corruption; Shopify extracted pieces while keeping a core Rails app.

Decision gravity. Incremental migration keeps each step reversible; big-bang rewrites (Netscape) are the classic failure. Data ownership transfer is the hardest, least reversible step.

Everyday analogy. Renovating a house room by room while living in it, instead of demolishing and rebuilding.

Common interview traps.

  • Splitting services before splitting data.
  • Dual-writes without reconciliation.
  • Not defining success metrics (latency, error rate parity) before cutover.

notes.title: API gateway and API composition
notes.html:
An API gateway is the single entry point that routes requests, handles auth, rate limiting and TLS, and can aggregate several service calls into one response (API composition). It saves mobile clients from chatting with 10 services.

Mechanism: the gateway/composer receives GET /order-page/42, calls Orders, Users and Inventory in parallel, merges results, and returns one payload. Variants: BFF (Backend For Frontend) per client type (mobile, web) so each gets a tailored shape; GraphQL gateway that lets the client choose fields. Handle partial failure: timeouts per call (for example 200 ms), fallbacks for non-critical data, and a total deadline.

suspend fun orderPage(id: String) = coroutineScope {
    val order = async { orders.get(id) }
    val user  = async { users.getFor(id) }
    val stock = async { withTimeoutOrNull(200) { inventory.get(id) } }   // optional data
    OrderPage(order.await(), user.await(), stock.await())
}

Worked example. Sequential: 3 calls x 60 ms = 180 ms. Parallel: max(60, 60, 60) = about 65 ms. With a 200 ms budget and the inventory service at p99 = 400 ms, the page returns without stock info rather than failing.

Industry examples. Netflix Zuul/Falcor then GraphQL federation, Kong, AWS API Gateway, Envoy/Ambassador, Apollo Federation (Airbnb, Expedia), BFF pattern at SoundCloud and Spotify. Joins across services in reports use CQRS read models instead of composition at scale.

Decision gravity. A gateway becomes a bottleneck and "god service" if business logic creeps in; keep it thin. Cross-service joins in memory do not scale beyond small result sets; use a precomputed read model if you need large joins or sorting across services.

Everyday analogy. A hotel concierge who calls the restaurant, taxi and tickets desk at once and brings you one answer.

Common interview traps.

  • Sequential calls instead of parallel.
  • No timeouts or fallback, so the slowest service dictates failure.
  • Putting domain logic in the gateway.

notes.title: Service mesh
notes.html:
A service mesh adds a network layer that handles service-to-service concerns (mTLS, retries, timeouts, load balancing, traffic shifting, metrics) outside application code. Typically each pod gets a sidecar proxy (Envoy) that all traffic passes through; a control plane (Istio, Linkerd, Consul Connect) pushes config.

Mechanism: app calls http://payments; the local sidecar intercepts it, picks a healthy endpoint (client-side load balancing), enforces mTLS identity, applies retry/timeout/circuit-breaker policy, records latency and traces, and forwards. Policies are declarative: canary 5% to v2, fault injection, locality-aware routing. Trade-offs: extra hop (about 1 to 3 ms p99 added per proxy pair), CPU and memory per sidecar (about 50 to 100 MB each: 1,000 pods = 50 to 100 GB), operational complexity. Newer "ambient"/sidecar-less modes (Istio ambient, Cilium) reduce overhead.

# Istio: 90/10 canary and retry policy
apiVersion: networking.istio.io/v1
kind: VirtualService
metadata: {name: payments}
spec:
  hosts: [payments]
  http:
  - route:
    - {destination: {host: payments, subset: v1}, weight: 90}
    - {destination: {host: payments, subset: v2}, weight: 10}
    retries: {attempts: 2, perTryTimeout: 1s, retryOn: "5xx,connect-failure"}
    timeout: 3s

Worked example. Rolling out mTLS to 300 services without a mesh means changing 300 codebases and languages. With a mesh: one PeerAuthentication policy. Retry policy: 2 retries x 1 s on a service already overloaded multiplies load by 3; set a retry budget (retries as less than 20% of requests).

Industry examples. Lyft created Envoy; Google/IBM/Lyft created Istio; Linkerd (Buoyant) is lightweight; Netflix used client libraries (Ribbon, Hystrix) before meshes; Uber and Airbnb run custom meshes.

Decision gravity. Adopting a mesh is a significant platform decision, semi one-way (policies and tooling become part of everything). Worth it at about 50+ services across many languages; overkill for 5 services where a library (Resilience4j) suffices.

Everyday analogy. Every office gets a mail clerk who handles envelopes, tracking and ID checks for all letters, so staff only write the letter.

Common interview traps.

  • Proposing a mesh for a small system.
  • Forgetting the latency and resource overhead.
  • Stacking retries at app, sidecar and gateway (retry amplification).
  • Mixing up mesh (east-west, service to service) with API gateway (north-south, client to system).

notes.title: Data ownership and consistency across services
notes.html:
Each service owns its data; others ask through an API or subscribe to events. No cross-service joins and no shared tables.

Techniques:

  • Database per service (can be separate schemas on one cluster early on).
  • Event-carried state transfer: a service keeps a local read-only copy of the fields it needs (for example customer_name) from events, so it can answer without calling.
  • Sagas for cross-service workflows and outbox to publish reliably.
  • Reference data by id, resolve at the edge via composition.
  • Reporting: stream all services to a warehouse (CDC to Snowflake/BigQuery/ClickHouse).

Worked example. Order list screen needs customer names for 50 orders. Naive: 50 calls to Users (50 x 5 ms = 250 ms, or one batch call 10 ms). Better: Orders keeps a customer_name copy updated from CustomerRenamed events; a rename takes about 200 ms to propagate, and the list needs no remote call.

Industry examples. Amazon's rule that teams expose only service interfaces, Uber's domain gateways, Netflix's data pipeline (Keystone) for analytics, Zalando's event-first integration.

Decision gravity. Shared database is a trap that is quick now and permanent coupling later. Choosing eventual consistency on purpose requires product buy-in on stale data.

Everyday analogy. Each department keeps its own filing cabinet; they send memos to update copies rather than rummaging in each other's drawers.

Common interview traps.

  • Shared DB "just for reads" (still couples schemas).
  • Distributed joins at request time at scale.
  • Claiming strong consistency across services without 2PC and its costs.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Monolith: simplest, fastest, ACID; scale horizontally behind a load balancer; fine up to dozens of engineers.
  • Microservices: independent deploy and scale per team, but pay latency, partial failure, eventual consistency and heavy ops; one-way door.
  • Modular monolith: strict module boundaries, own tables per module, enforced by tools; the best default and the best stepping stone.
  • Choose by team size, scaling shape, ops maturity; extract services on evidence, not fashion.
  • Migrate with the strangler fig: route gradually, shadow, compare, roll back via routing; move data last and carefully.
  • API gateway handles north-south concerns and can compose calls in parallel with timeouts and fallbacks; use BFF or GraphQL per client; keep it thin.
  • Service mesh (Envoy sidecars plus control plane) gives mTLS, retries, traffic shifting and telemetry for east-west traffic; costs latency and resources; useful at many services.
  • Own data per service; share by events, composition and CDC; avoid shared databases and distributed joins.

questions.promptHtml: What are the real trade-offs between a monolith and microservices?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you see microservices as an organisational tool with a runtime cost, not a default.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A monolith is one deployable with usually one database: simple to build, debug and test, with free cross-feature transactions and nanosecond calls. Microservices split into independently deployed services that own their data and talk over the network. The benefit is team and scaling independence; the price is latency, partial failure, distributed data consistency and a platform investment (tracing, CI/CD per service, on-call). I choose microservices for team scaling or very different scaling shapes, never for fashion.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The latency and availability tax: 6 services in a chain, each 99.9% available, gives 0.999^6 = 99.4% (about 52 h downtime/year vs 8.8 h for one). The combined p99 is also above any single service's p99, and careless retries cause retry storms.

Monolith:     Client -> LB -> [instance 1, instance 2] -> one DB
Microservice: Client -> Gateway -> Orders -> (Orders DB)
                                -> Users  -> (Users DB)

A monolith still scales horizontally behind a load balancer if it is stateless.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling a monolith "legacy" or "bad".
  • Splitting services but sharing one database.
  • Forgetting the platform cost.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. When does a monolith break down? -> Roughly 30 to 50 engineers in one codebase, deploys blocking each other, or one part needing a different scaling shape.
  2. Is it reversible? -> Starting monolith is; premature microservices is a one-way door.
  3. How do you get consistency across services? -> Sagas and eventual consistency, not cross-DB transactions.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "microservices scale better". Senior: org structure, availability arithmetic, the platform bill and data ownership.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A 6-person team with 25 services spent more time on deployments and tracing than features.

questions.promptHtml: What is a modular monolith and why is it often the best default?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks you know the middle path with clear boundaries.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A modular monolith is one deployable made of modules with strict boundaries: each module exposes a public interface, hides its internals and its tables, and does not reach into others. You get local calls and one DB transaction, but also clear ownership. Boundaries drawn wrong are cheap to redraw inside a monolith and very expensive across services. When a module needs independent scaling, I extract it behind its existing interface.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Enforce boundaries with build tooling: separate Gradle/Maven modules or package visibility, architecture tests (ArchUnit), and a rule that modules talk through interfaces or in-process events, never by joining another module's tables.

[orders]--interface-->[billing]   one process, one deploy
   |                      |
 orders schema        billing schema (same DB, separate schemas)

Example: 40 engineers, 6 modules, 1 deploy a day. Extracting search took a week because its interface already existed.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Modules sharing tables, so extraction becomes impossible.
  • Treating it as a big ball of mud with folders.
  • No enforcement, so boundaries rot.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you enforce boundaries? -> Module build separation, architecture tests, schema ownership.
  2. Team size sweet spot? -> About 10 to 100 engineers.
  3. How do modules communicate? -> Public interfaces or in-process domain events.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "monolith with packages". Senior: enforced boundaries, data ownership per module, extraction path.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team extracted billing in two weeks because the module already owned its tables.

questions.contextHtml: Series A startup, 8 engineers, one Rails/Spring monolith, 300 req/s peak, 99.95% SLO. The new CTO wants to move to 20 microservices "to scale". Deploys are weekly because of a flaky test suite, not because of coupling. The only real hotspot is image processing that spikes 10x and needs GPUs. Hiring plan: 20 engineers in 12 months.
questions.promptHtml: What architecture do you propose, and how do you push back?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Yes, microservices scale." or "No, never split".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the current bottleneck (CPU, DB, deploy cadence)? What do the deploy failures look like? Which domains change independently? What is the ops capacity?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Fix the flaky tests and move to daily deploys; add a read replica if the DB is the hotspot.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: problem is test hygiene and one workload shape, not the architecture.
  4. How I'd verify: deploy frequency, failure causes, CPU profile per endpoint.
  5. Root cause: a scaling-shape mismatch for one workload only.
  6. Fix: modular monolith with enforced boundaries; extract only media-processing as a queue-fed worker service on GPU nodes. Everything else stays. Revisit when team passes ~30 engineers.
  7. Prevention: an ADR listing the triggers for the next extraction (team size, independent release need, scaling shape).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: 20 services means 20 pipelines, tracing, on-call: with 8 engineers that is the whole team.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Investor asks for "microservices"? -> Show the extraction path and the one extracted service.
  • Different teams step on each other later? -> Module ownership first, extract on evidence.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team of 10 spent a year on a service split and shipped no features, then merged half back.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: follows fashion.
  • Hire: modular monolith with one extraction.
  • Strong hire: explicit triggers, root-cause of slow deploys, cost of microservices.

questions.promptHtml: What does an API gateway do, and how does API composition differ from a gateway?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Gateways turn into god services; the interviewer looks for the line between plumbing and business logic.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A gateway is the single entry point handling cross-cutting concerns: routing, TLS, authentication, rate limiting, request shaping. API composition is aggregating data from several services into one response (a BFF or composer). Composition calls services in parallel with timeouts and returns partial results on failure. I keep the gateway thin; business logic does not belong there.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Latency math: 3 sequential calls x 60 ms = 180 ms; in parallel about 65 ms. With a 200 ms budget and an inventory service at p99 400 ms, the composer returns the page without stock info rather than failing. In-memory joins across services do not scale beyond small result sets; for big joins or sorting use a precomputed read model.

Client -> Gateway(auth, rate limit) -> Composer -> [Orders | Users | Inventory] in parallel

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Business rules creeping into the gateway.
  • Sequential fan-out calls.
  • No per-call timeout or fallback.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is a BFF? -> A gateway per client type (web, mobile) shaping responses for it.
  2. How do you page and sort across services? -> You cannot join in memory at scale; use a read model.
  3. Gateway as single point of failure? -> Run many instances behind an LB; keep it stateless.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists features. Senior discusses latency budgets, partial responses and keeping it logic-free.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A gateway with pricing rules became the release bottleneck for 5 teams.

questions.contextHtml: Checkout calls Cart -> Pricing -> Inventory -> Tax -> Payments -> Notifications in sequence. Each service is 99.9% available with p50 20 ms and p99 50 ms. Checkout SLO: 99.9% availability and p99 under 200 ms. The monitoring shows checkout availability at 99.4% and p99 at 310 ms. A 7th service called Loyalty is proposed in the chain.
questions.promptHtml: Why is the SLO missed and what do you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale each service" or "add retries".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which calls truly need to be synchronous? Are calls sequential or independent? Are there retries? What does each call contribute to p99?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Make Notifications async via a queue; call independent services (Pricing, Inventory, Tax) in parallel.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: serial chain compounding; retry amplification; a slow dependency's tail.
  4. How I'd verify: distributed traces (critical path), per-hop p99, retry counts.
  5. Root cause: 0.999^6 = 99.4% exactly matches the observed availability; tail latencies add across serial calls.
  6. Fix: parallelise independent calls (latency to the max, not the sum), make non-critical steps async or degradable (loyalty points added later), put timeouts and a circuit breaker on each call, merge chatty services that always change together.
  7. Prevention: latency budget per hop; adding a service to a sync path needs a review.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: not retries without a budget; they multiply load on an already slow service.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Which services can fail open? -> Loyalty, recommendations; not Payments.
  • Merge services? -> If they deploy together and share data, yes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A seven-hop chain hit 97% availability; making three hops async brought it back to the SLO.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale or retry.
  • Hire: calculates 0.999^6 and parallelises.
  • Strong hire: async non-critical steps, circuit breakers, merging chatty services.

questions.contextHtml:
Orders service and Reporting service both read and write the customers table in one shared Postgres. Reporting added a nightly job that does UPDATE customers SET segment = ... with a long transaction. The Orders team can't add a NOT NULL column because Reporting breaks, and last Tuesday the job locked rows for 40 minutes:

ERROR: deadlock detected / lock wait timeout on customers
Orders p99: 120 ms -> 9 s

"We are microservices, but ..."
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong architecturally, and what is the plan?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add an index" or "run the job at night" (it did run at night).

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who owns customers? How fresh must Reporting data be? Which columns does Reporting need?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Move the job to a read replica, shorten the transaction (batch updates).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: shared-table coupling; long transaction lock contention.
  4. How I'd verify: pg_stat_activity, lock waits, who writes which columns.
  5. Root cause: a shared database means hidden coupling in schema and locking.
  6. Fix: Customers service owns the table. Others get data via API or events (CustomerRenamed), keeping their own copy (a rename propagates in about 200 ms). Reporting uses CDC into its own store and writes segment through the owner's API.
  7. Prevention: per-service DB credentials and schemas so cross-service access fails; review rule "no foreign tables".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: copies are eventually consistent; product must accept stale names for moments.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• 50 orders need customer names? -> Batch call or local copy, never 50 remote calls.
  • Cannot do it all at once? -> Start by revoking write access for non-owners.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A shared schema survived 4 years until a column migration needed 7 teams to coordinate.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tweak the job.
  • Hire: data ownership and events or API.
  • Strong hire: staged revocation of access, CDC, stale-data trade-off.

questions.contextHtml: Billing lives in a 10-year-old monolith (8k invoices/hour, money involved). Leadership wants a billing service in 10 weeks. Someone proposes a rewrite and a weekend cutover. Past shadow experiments in another team showed 0.5% mismatches on rounding.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Big-bang rewrite and cutover.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Who owns the billing tables? Can we replicate them? What is the rollback tolerance? Which callers exist?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed; this is planned. Put a routing facade in front of billing calls first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: hidden business rules in the legacy code, data ownership transfer, rounding differences.
  4. How I'd verify: shadow reads with diffing.
  5. Root cause of the risk: big-bang rewrites hide unknowns until cutover.
  6. Fix: strangler fig. Week 1: build the service, replicate data with Debezium. Week 3: shadow-read 100% and diff (fix the 0.02% mismatches). Week 5: route 5% of writes. Week 7: 100%. Week 9: delete the monolith code. Rollback at any step is a routing change.
  7. Prevention: feature flag per tenant, reconciliation job daily.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: the hardest, least reversible step is transferring data ownership; do it last and with a reverse-sync window.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Mismatch of 0.5%? -> Do not proceed until explained; money differences compound.
  • Both write paths active? -> Single writer per record at any time; route by tenant.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A weekend cutover without shadow mode double-billed 3% of customers.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: rewrite and cutover.
  • Hire: strangler with incremental routing.
  • Strong hire: shadow diff, rollback by routing, ownership transfer last.

questions.promptHtml: What does a service mesh give you, what does it cost, and when is it not worth it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates platform-aware engineers from those who adopt tools by hype.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A service mesh moves service-to-service networking into sidecar or node proxies: mTLS, retries, timeouts, traffic shifting, and telemetry without code changes. With 300 services in many languages, enforcing mTLS means one policy instead of 300 code changes. The cost is latency per hop, resource overhead, operational complexity and a platform team. It is worth it around 50+ services across languages; for 5 services a library like Resilience4j is enough.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
App A -> [proxy] ==mTLS==> [proxy] -> App B
            ^ control plane pushes policy, certs, routes

Dangerous defaults: 2 retries on a service already overloaded triples load. Use a retry budget (retries under 20% of requests), timeouts shorter than the caller's deadline, and circuit breaking. Mesh handles transport-level concerns; it does not replace idempotency or business-level resilience.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mesh retries plus application retries multiply.
  • Adopting without a platform team.
  • Believing it solves data consistency.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Sidecar vs ambient/node proxy? -> Sidecars cost memory per pod; node-level proxies reduce cost with different isolation trade-offs (verify per mesh).
  2. Canary traffic? -> Weighted routes in the mesh.
  3. What does it not fix? -> Slow queries, bad API design, distributed transactions.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "mTLS and retries". Senior: costs, retry budgets, one-way-ness and when a library suffices.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A mesh default of 3 retries amplified a slow-dependency incident 4x.

questions.contextHtml:
Pricing service p99 rose from 80 ms to 4 s after a deploy. Within 3 minutes Orders, Cart and Checkout all alarm. Traffic into Pricing: 5k/s normal, 16k/s now. Mesh config: 3 retries on 5xx and timeouts, app SDK also retries 2 times; per-try timeout 2 s. CPU on Pricing is 98%.

pricing  rps_in=16210  5xx=41%  p99=4.1s
checkout rps_out_to_pricing=15980

Someone suggests scaling Pricing 4x.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do right now and what is the root cause?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Scale only, never touching retries.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What changed (deploy, config)? Where are retries configured? Is there a circuit breaker? Can we roll back?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the Pricing deploy; disable mesh retries to Pricing; shed load (rate limit non-critical callers); serve cached prices.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: deploy slowed Pricing; retries (3 mesh x 3 app = up to 9x) amplified load; thread pool saturation; DB slow.
  4. How I'd verify: compare rps in vs original demand; traces for retry counts; deploy diff.
  5. Root cause: a slow dependency plus stacked retries produced a retry storm; 5k/s demand became 16k/s and kept it saturated.
  6. Fix: retry budget (retries below 20% of requests), a single retry layer, backoff with jitter, timeouts below the caller's deadline, circuit breakers, load shedding on Pricing.
  7. Prevention: a game-day for slow dependencies; alert on retry ratio.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: scaling 4x without fixing retries only raises the ceiling; the cause remains.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Roll back impossible? -> Throttle callers, cached fallback.
  • Retries needed for blips? -> Keep one, budgeted, idempotent calls only.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An overloaded service recovered in 2 minutes once retries were disabled, after 40 minutes of scaling attempts.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale up.
  • Hire: spots retry amplification and removes it.
  • Strong hire: budgets, single retry layer, breaker, shed and cache.

questions.contextHtml: Order list screen shows 50 orders with customer names. Orders and Users are separate services. Current implementation calls Users 50 times (5 ms each, sequential): 250 ms. Users has a rate limit that is hit at peak. A rename currently shows instantly. Product says the list must load under 100 ms.
questions.promptHtml: Design the data flow and explain the consistency trade-off.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Join the two databases".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How stale can a name be (seconds is fine)? Is the name legal data or display only? List size growth? Does Users publish events?
  2. Immediate mitigation: One batch call (GET /users?ids=..., about 10 ms) in place of 50.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: batch call vs local copy vs read model.
  4. How I'd verify: measure batch latency under peak and the rate limit.
  5. Root cause: N+1 remote calls.
  6. Fix: Orders keeps a customer_name copy updated from CustomerRenamed events; a rename takes about 200 ms to propagate; list needs no remote call, and Users outage no longer breaks the list. Backfill the copy via a one-time snapshot plus events.
  7. Prevention: copies carry a version; reconcile job; events are an API contract.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not share tables; stale names for about 200 ms must be accepted by product. For legal documents, snapshot the name at order time instead.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Event lost? -> Outbox plus periodic reconcile.
  • Much larger sorts or joins by customer fields? -> A dedicated read model.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A list screen with 50 remote calls was the top cause of timeouts until local copies cut it to one query.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: shared DB.
  • Hire: batch call or local copy.
  • Strong hire: explains the staleness contract, backfill and reconciliation.

questions.contextHtml: In a 40-engineer modular monolith, the search module needs independent scaling: it uses 70% of the CPU on instances and its indexing batch jobs slow down checkout. Search reads products and orders_summary tables owned by other modules via direct SQL joins. Deploys are daily. You have 4 weeks.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Copy the code to a new repo and point it at the same DB.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does search need (data, freshness)? Who calls it? Is the interface already narrow?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Run search indexing on dedicated instances or a different schedule, or throttle batch jobs.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: the direct SQL joins are the blocker, not the code.
  4. How I'd verify: list all SQL touching other modules' tables.
  5. Root cause: the module boundary leaks via shared tables.
  6. Fix: first replace joins with owning modules' interfaces and domain events (still in-process); build the search index from events (CDC or outbox); then deploy the same module as a separate process behind its existing interface; route via gateway with a flag; keep the old path for rollback.
  7. Prevention: architecture tests prevent new cross-module SQL.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not split the DB first; the order is code boundary, then data flow, then deployment.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Search index drift? -> Reconcile job.
  • Extracted service goes down? -> Fallback to a cached/limited search; degrade gracefully.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: The extraction took one week since the boundary work had been done earlier; teams without it took months.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: copy code to new repo.
  • Hire: fix boundary then extract.
  • Strong hire: event-fed index, flag with rollback, architecture tests.

questions.contextHtml: The API gateway ran product-page composition: calls Catalog, Pricing, Inventory, Reviews sequentially, and contains discount rules written by 3 teams. Black Friday: gateway p99 3.8 s, error rate 6%, and a Reviews slowdown (p99 400 ms) took down the whole page. Deploys of the gateway needed approval from 5 teams and blocked a hotfix for 6 hours.
questions.promptHtml: Write the review: contributing factors and fixes.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Scale the gateway".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What is the latency budget? Which data is mandatory? What is in the gateway code?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Drop Reviews from the response when its deadline passes; cache; rate limit.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: sequential calls (4 x ~60 ms vs parallel 65 ms); no timeouts or fallback; business logic in the gateway as a shared bottleneck.
  4. How I'd verify: traces on the critical path; threads blocked waiting on Reviews.
  5. Root cause: the gateway acted as a god service: composition without timeouts and domain logic.
  6. Fix: parallel calls with per-call deadlines and partial responses (200 ms budget: Reviews missing just hides the stars); move discount rules into Pricing; split into BFFs per client team; precomputed read model for the product page if joins grow.
  7. Prevention: gateway lint rule: no domain logic; per-route SLOs; load tests with a slow dependency.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: do not just add instances; the lock-step ownership remains.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Reviews required by contract? -> Cache last-known value with a staleness flag.
  • Who owns BFFs? -> The consuming team.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A gateway that held pricing rules became a 5-team deploy queue; moving rules out cut change lead time from days to hours.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: scale up.
  • Hire: parallelism with timeouts and partial responses.
  • Strong hire: removes logic, BFF ownership, per-route SLOs.
